title: Project: Bank / ATM Simulator
learningGoals: design a program as small functions that take a value and return the updated value (no globals)
validate every input (not a number, negative, zero, too large) before using it
persist a single value in a text file with `fprintf` / `fscanf`
add a PIN check with a limited number of tries

youtube.title: Build an ATM in C (Without Breaking the Bank) | EP 85
youtube.description: Withdraw minus 5000 rupees and get richer? Not in our ATM. We build a full bank ATM simulator in C with balance, deposit and withdraw, save the balance to a file, and validate every single input. Full code, explained line by line. Chapters: 0:00 Withdraw without breaking the bank · 0:20 The plan · 0:50 Saving the balance · 2:00 Reading a safe amount · 3:05 Deposit and withdraw · 4:15 The menu · 4:50 Demo · 5:40 Bug of the Day · 7:00 Challenge

scenes.onScreen: A broken ATM: withdraw -5000, balance goes UP to 15000; withdraw 50000, balance -40000
scenes.animation: Cash-register "cha-ching" then alarm siren; Xecxec faints
scenes.narration: Welcome to the worst ATM in Goa. Balance: 10,000 rupees. Let's withdraw minus 5,000. "Please collect minus 5,000". And the balance goes up to 15,000! Now withdraw 50,000. Balance: minus 40,000. The bank manager has fainted. Today we build an ATM that checks everything.

scenes.onScreen: Plan: `balance` lives in main → passed into deposit/withdraw → new balance returned → saved to `balance.txt`. Rule card: "Never trust input"
scenes.animation: Arrows loop from main to function and back; stamp SFX on the rule
scenes.narration: Here's the plan. The balance lives in main, as a local variable. When you deposit or withdraw, main passes the balance into a function, and the function returns the new balance. That's call by value from EP 38, used on purpose. No globals this time. After every change, we save the balance to a small text file, so it survives a restart. And one rule above all: never trust input. Every amount gets checked before it touches the balance.

scenes.animation: Butter highlights; text file icon shows `12500.00` inside
scenes.narration: [HL 3] Line three: the file name. [HL 4] Line four: MIN_BALANCE, 500 rupees, the minimum the bank wants you to keep. A named constant, from EP 10, instead of a magic number. [HL 6-7] loadBalance starts with a default opening balance of 10,000 for the very first run. [HL 8] Open balance dot txt for reading. [HL 9] If the file exists, [HL 10-12] fscanf reads one double with percent l f. If that fails, say someone typed rubbish into the file, we fall back to 10,000. [HL 13] Close it. [HL 15] Return the balance. [HL 18] saveBalance takes the balance as a parameter. [HL 19-23] Open for writing, and check for NULL. [HL 24] fprintf writes it with two decimal places. Because this is a text file, you can open it in Notepad and read it. That's handy for one number. For many records, like last episode, a binary file is better.

scenes.animation: Butter highlights; bad inputs (abc, -50, 0) bounce off a shield
scenes.narration: [HL 28-31] clearInput, the same helper from EP 84. [HL 33] readAmount: the security guard of our ATM. Its only job is to return a valid amount. [HL 35] while 1 means "keep asking until we get a good answer". [HL 36] Ask for the amount. [HL 37] Two checks in one line. scanf must return 1, meaning it really read a number, and amount must be greater than zero. Because of the double ampersand, if scanf fails, C doesn't even look at amount. [HL 38-39] If both pass, clear the Enter key and return the amount. [HL 41-42] If not, clear the bad line and say "Enter a positive number". Then the loop asks again. abc, rejected. Minus 50, rejected. Zero, rejected. Every function that needs an amount calls readAmount, so the checking is written in one place.

scenes.animation: Butter highlights; tracker for balance and amount; MIN_BALANCE line drawn on a bar
scenes.narration: [HL 46] deposit takes the current balance. [HL 47] Gets a safe amount from readAmount. [TRACK amount=2500] [HL 48] Adds it. [TRACK balance=12500] [HL 49-50] Prints a receipt and returns the new balance. [HL 53] withdraw also takes the balance. [HL 54] Safe amount again. [HL 55] The second check: would the balance drop below 500? [TRACK amount=20000] If balance minus amount is less than MIN_BALANCE, [HL 56-57] decline, and return the balance unchanged. [HL 59-61] Otherwise subtract, say "Please collect", and return the new balance. [TRACK amount=4000] [TRACK balance=8500] One honest note: we use double for money to keep this simple. Real banking software stores paise as whole numbers, because decimals can't always be stored exactly. You saw that kind of rounding in EP 08.

scenes.animation: Butter highlights; loop arrow around the switch
scenes.narration: [HL 65] main loads the balance once. [HL 67] Welcome message. [HL 68-75] The same safe menu loop from EP 84: check that scanf read a number, otherwise clear and continue. [HL 77] Option 1 prints the balance. [HL 78] Option 2: balance equals deposit of balance, then save. See how the returned value is stored back into balance? Without that assignment, the deposit would vanish, exactly like EP 38's bug. [HL 79] Option 3, the same for withdraw. [HL 80] Option 4 says goodbye. [HL 83] Loop until 4.

scenes.animation: Typing SFX; note notes slide out of an ATM slot on withdraw
scenes.narration: Compile with gcc atm dot c, dash o, atm, and run. Check balance: 10,000. Deposit 2,500. Now withdraw, and try to break it. Minus 50: rejected. a b c: rejected. 20,000: declined, you must keep 500. 4,000: please collect. Balance: 8,500. Exit, and open balance dot txt: 8500 point 00, saved. Run it again, and the ATM remembers.
Why did the ATM need a break? It had too many withdrawals and no deposit of energy left.

scenes.onScreen: `atmbug.c`: no validation; negative and huge withdrawals; fixed version
scenes.animation: Balance counter spins the wrong way; fix shows checks as gates, mint tick
scenes.narration: Today's bug: no input validation. Here's the ATM from the cold open, cut down. It reads the amount with scanf and subtracts it. No checks at all. The compiler is perfectly happy, even with dash Wall. It is valid C. It's just a terrible ATM. Minus 5,000 makes the balance go up to 15,000. 50,000 makes it minus 40,000. And type letters, and scanf fails, amount stays unset, and you get garbage. The fix adds two gates. Gate one: if scanf didn't return 1, or the amount is zero or less, print "Invalid amount" and stop. Gate two: if the amount is more than the balance minus 500, print "Declined". Only after both gates do we touch the balance. In real software, most security problems start right here: with input nobody checked.

scenes.onScreen: Challenge card: 4-digit PIN, 3 tries, then "Card blocked"
scenes.narration: Your challenge: add a PIN check. Write a function checkPin that allows three tries to enter the PIN 4321. It returns 1 if the PIN is right, and 0 after three wrong tries. In main, call it before the menu. If it returns 0, print "Card blocked. Visit your branch." and end the program. Hint: a for loop from 1 to 3, and remember to clear the input after each try.

scenes.animation: Graduation cap drops onto Xecxec; sign-off jingle
scenes.narration: Two projects done! Next episode is the grand finale: exam prep, the questions examiners love, and a sneak peek at what comes after C. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
No compiler warning, even with `-Wall`. Wrong output for input `-5000`:

Amount to withdraw (Rs): -5000
Please collect Rs -5000.00
Balance: Rs 15000.00

For input `50000`:

Amount to withdraw (Rs): 50000
Please collect Rs 50000.00
Balance: Rs -40000.00

(For input `abc`, scanf fails and `amount` is never set, so the output is garbage that changes from machine to machine.)
bug.why: the compiler only checks that code is valid C, not that input makes sense, so the program itself must reject non-numbers, non-positive amounts and amounts larger than the allowed balance.

pun: Why did the ATM need a break? Too many withdrawals, and no deposit of energy left.
challenge: Add `int checkPin(void)`: three tries to enter PIN 4321, returns 1 on success, 0 after three wrong tries. Call it before the menu; on 0 print "Card blocked. Visit your branch." and end.

shorts.title: The Worst ATM in Goa
shorts.script: Withdraw minus 5,000 rupees, and your balance goes up to 15,000. Withdraw 50,000, and you're at minus 40,000. This ATM compiles with zero warnings. It's valid C. It just never checks the input. In episode 85, we build one that does.
shorts.caption: Valid code, broken bank.

shorts.title: Input Validation in 30 Seconds
shorts.script: Two checks make input safe. One: did scanf return 1? If not, the user typed something that isn't a number. Two: is the value in range, like greater than zero? If either fails, clear the line and ask again. Put this in one function, readAmount, and call it everywhere. Write the checking once, use it everywhere.
shorts.onScreen: IS IT A NUMBER? IS IT IN RANGE?
shorts.caption: Two checks every C program needs.

shorts.title: The Bug That Robs the Bank
shorts.script: This withdraw code reads the amount and subtracts it. No checks. Minus 5,000 adds money. 50,000 sends you negative. Letters give garbage. The fix: gate one, reject anything that isn't a positive number. Gate two, decline if it would drop below the minimum balance. Only then touch the balance.
shorts.caption: Most security bugs start with unchecked input.

shorts.title: The Tired ATM
shorts.hook: an ATM yawning, Xecxec fanning it
shorts.script: Why did the ATM need a break? It had too many withdrawals and no deposit of energy left.
shorts.caption: Even machines need a holiday.

shorts.title: Quiz: Will It Withdraw?
shorts.script: Balance is 1,000 rupees. The minimum balance is 500. You try to withdraw 600. What happens? A: Please collect 600. B: Declined. C: Enter a positive number. The answer is B. 1,000 minus 600 is 400, which is below 500.
shorts.caption: Comment your answer before the reveal.
